extracted.intended_audience: authors querying literary agents (aspiring and self-published writers seeking representation)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing effective agent query letters that prompt manuscript requests, covering structure, personalization, formatting, comps, author platform, and submission etiquette across fiction and nonfiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization / Agent fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Address the query to the agent's name and show you've done your homework about their tastes (e.g., reference MSWL, agency site, or a client title).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baseline requirement is addressing the agent by name; include one or two sentences at the start showing you researched them (e.g., 'I saw on MSWL that you're looking for...'). Personalization signals you aren't sending a shotgun 'Dear Agent' letter and makes agents likelier to spend extra time on your query. If you met the agent at an event, mention it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow agent submission guidelines exactly
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow any specific salutation, formatting, subject line, materials requested, and follow-up instructions the agent or agency posts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents may specify preferences (e.g., how to address them). Failure to follow stated guidelines (wrong salutation or format) is an instant negative. If an agent states a response time or 'do not nudge', respect it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-line metadata up front (title, genre, word count, comps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put title, genre and word count and comp titles at the front of the letter so the agent immediately knows what the book is and where it might sit in the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents like seeing this information early — some recommend literally at the top. State comps in first paragraph and try to include one title the agent represented. Put book title in CAPITAL LETTERS as a formatting convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative titles (comps) — current and relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Use current, contemporary comparable titles that help place your book in the market; ideally include one comp the agent or agency represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't use bestsellers as lazy comps or books published over 2-3 years ago; be current. Read every comp you cite and be ready to explain how each is like and not like your book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong hook / logline
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with a compelling hook or logline that intrigues and communicates the central premise succinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single-sentence logline before the plot paragraph can be an efficient way to hook the reader. For nonfiction, an intriguing anecdotal hook can work well (e.g., a striking personal moment that introduced the topic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Main character and stakes up front
rubrics_metrics.description: Show who the protagonist is early and give the agent a reason to care — brief character description (2–3 sentences) before introducing the inciting incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents want to root for a character; establish the protagonist’s wants, situation, and stakes so subsequent chaos feels meaningful. This applies across genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise plot/premise: problem/obstacle/challenge/stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize the plot in one (maybe two) short paragraphs focusing on protagonist's goal, the obstacle, the challenge, and the stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format recommendation: '[Protagonist] wants [motivation], but [obstacle] gets in the way. They'll have to [challenge] if they're ever going to achieve [stakes].' Don’t provide a full synopsis or the ending; one to two paragraphs is ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid spoilers / don't give away the ending
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not give away the entire plot or ending in the query letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A query is meant to intrigue enough to request pages, not to summarize every plot beat. Avoid full synopses or revealing major spoilers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity over vagueness / avoid clichés and sweeping claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Be specific about the setup, conflict and stakes; avoid vague claims ('sweeping love story') and rhetorical questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents prefer details that distinguish your book from others. Replace vague marketing language with concrete specifics about character, conflict and plot twists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author bio / 'Cook' section: relevant credentials and platform
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a short author paragraph with relevant writing credentials and platform (publications, awards, blog/social metrics), and a brief note about why you are the right person to write this book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep this brief and relevant. Mention platform metrics if helpful (e.g., blog unique viewers). For nonfiction, indicate expertise and readiness (e.g., completed manuscript or proposal). If you have no publishing credits, a short personal note about why you wrote the book is sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: State available materials (manuscript, proposal, sample pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify what you are attaching or offering (complete manuscript vs. proposal vs. sample chapters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially important for nonfiction where either a proposal or a manuscript may be expected. Agents appreciate knowing where you are in the process (complete manuscript attached, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Target audience and commercial potential
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the book's target audience and why it will appeal to that market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about who will read the book and how it fits commercially; this helps agents assess marketability. Don’t make unrealistic sales promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Query structure: Hook, Book, Cook (clear sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize the query into clear functional parts: hook/lead, book summary (plot/premise), and author info/platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One recommended format: Paragraph 1 — metadata (title/word count/comps/personalization); Paragraphs 2–3 — book summary; Final paragraph(s) — author bio and what materials you’ve submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and formatting conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the query short (industry guidance: ~300 words / no more than one page) and formatted cleanly (single-spaced, left-justified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting specifics mentioned include single-spaced, left justified, two spaces between paragraphs, no tabs/indents, no bold/underlining, book title in CAPITALS. Put the query in the body of the email (not as an attachment) unless requested. Follow any agent-specific formatting preferences if stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Email etiquette: subject line, body placement, attachments
rubrics_metrics.description: When emailing, follow the agent's instructions for subject line, paste the letter into the body of the email, and avoid attachments unless requested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject line example: 'Query - Title of Book - Name of Author.' Do not send queries as attachments unless the agent asks for one; some agents print queries, so body placement helps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up etiquette and response expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect agents' stated response times; typical advice is to wait ~3 months before following up unless the agency specifies otherwise; do not repeatedly nudge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agent requests no follow-ups, treat silence as a pass. Exception: if you receive an offer (rep or publication), notify agents who have requested pages and give a short timeframe (usually 10 days–2 weeks) to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research for agent/press-specific fit (don’t query wrong agent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Query agents who represent your genre and type of book; sending the wrong genre to an agent will result in swift rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research each agent’s list and tastes. Reference relevant clients or books to demonstrate fit. Different agents/publishers may require different query styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not send generic shotgun queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid mass-sent, template 'Dear Agent' queries that show no personalization or research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic salutations and generic copycat language suggest a slapdash approach and reduce chances of success. Personalize each query to show intent and fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be professional, concise and avoid irrelevant personal info
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep tone professional and concise; do not volunteer unnecessary personal background or unrelated details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Queries are not cover letters about your life; include only what’s relevant to the book’s credibility or marketing (e.g., teaching experience for nonfiction). Avoid oversharing or including full life stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t query a whole series—focus on a single title
rubrics_metrics.description: Query for one title at a time; mention other works/series succinctly if relevant, but do not pitch an entire series in the initial query.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents generally expect a single-title pitch. You can note other titles or forthcoming works briefly, but the query's focus should be the one book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and manuscript preparation expectations (when applicable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use industry-accepted manuscript formatting when asked (e.g., double-spaced Times New Roman 12pt for sample pages/manuscript), and conform to any agent instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One contributor notes standard manuscript formatting (double-spaced, Times New Roman, one-inch margins, 12pt) — follow the agent's stated preferences for sample pages/manuscripts and use professional formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comps and reading the comps you cite
rubrics_metrics.description: Only cite comps you have read and be prepared to explain how each comp is comparable and how your book differs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As Michael I. states: 'Read every book you use as a comp' and take notes on similarities/differences; you'll need this for proposals and agent conversations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include minimal contact sign-off (name; avoid over-contacting information)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sign off professionally (first and last name); agents already have your email, so keep the sign-off simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One recommendation: include only first and last name in the query; do not clutter the sign-off with unnecessary contact details unless requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use platform metrics sensibly
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a platform (blog, social following), include specific, relevant metrics to demonstrate reach and potential audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metrics (e.g., '500 unique viewers a month') can add credibility for unknown authors; ensure numbers are honest and relevant to the book's audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone control: keep query letter tone appropriate to genre (avoid pulpy back-cover voice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Match the query’s tone to the manuscript’s tone and keep it professional — sell the story without turning it into pulpy back-cover copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may edit a query to ensure tone is suitable; queries that read like sensationalized blurbs can harm credibility. Preserve voice but remain pitch-appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence mindset and revision practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect rejections; keep revising queries and manuscripts and treat querying as a process requiring patience, perseverance, and continual improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many successful authors faced many rejections; use feedback, refine your query and pages, research agents thoroughly, and keep writing new projects if needed.
